prize_parts.citation: for the invention and realisation of optical lattice clocks, based on magic-wavelength trapping of many neutral atoms, reaching 10^-18 fractional uncertainty

statement.case_for: I keep B029 as my single preferred part, and the first round has strengthened rather than weakened it. The achievement is bounded: Katori's magic-wavelength lattice cancels the trap light shift for a transition held by many neutral atoms that are free of Doppler and recoil effects, and Ye's group turned this into strontium clocks at 10^-18 with the many-body and relativistic effects visible in the clock itself. Performance at that level has been reproduced and intercompared at JILA, RIKEN and Tokyo, PTB, SYRTE and NIST, and I regard that as the best maturity evidence anyone has put forward, better than a count of rankings. On the chair's first question, I think the 2005 and 2012 prizes leave the lattice clock as a separate achievement: the comb is the readout, and ion control gives single-ion clocks that trade statistics against systematics in a different way. The citation should say so by naming magic-wavelength trapping of many neutral atoms, and it should rest on demonstrated performance, not on the pending redefinition of the second. On the fallback question, I would turn to B018 first, with the Wineland overlap and the NIST and Monroe credit stated explicitly, and then B031.
statement.case_against: The overlap argument is legitimate and I cannot make it disappear: a sceptic can still read the lattice clock as the next refinement of a programme honoured in 2005 and 2012, and the strongest ion clocks (Al+) competed on accuracy. A two-name credit also leaves out Lemonde, Ludlow, Lisdat, Hinkley, Bloom and others who reached comparable accuracy. I rest the choice of Katori and Ye on origin and realisation, since Katori proposed the scheme and Ye's group took it to the lowest uncertainty and developed its many-body physics, but that is a judgement about priority, not a theorem. Finally, no one has yet used the clocks to find a deviation in a fundamental constant, so the prospective physics should not be written into the citation. If the committee finds the overlap with earlier prizes too large, B018 is where I would look, but it carries its own overlap with 2012.

responses.point: Kroll discloses a stay in John Hall's laboratory and the Hall and JILA environment around Ye, claims no direct tie to Katori or Ye, and writes new tests of fundamental physics and a path to redefining the second into his citation.
responses.response: I would treat his Hall stay as a disclosure that the committee records and not as a recusal, because it concerns the wider environment and not a collaboration, supervision or shared funding with either candidate, and because the same preference is held independently by Lindroth, Mehlig, Olsson, Pearce and now me. The chair asks whether the outcome would change without his vote, and it would not. Where I still differ from him is the wording: the tests of fundamental physics and the redefinition path are prospective, and I would prefer that the citation rest on the demonstrated 10^-18 performance and the lattice concept that made it possible.

responses.point: Lindroth says the 1e-18 milestone is shared among several species and groups, so the citation should name the lattice-clock concept and its realisation and not a record number, and she holds that the 2005 overlap is smaller than the ballots suggest because the comb is the readout.
responses.response: I agree and have changed my own wording on that basis. In round 1 I wrote about a fractional uncertainty of 10^-18 as the headline; I now think the numerical record is the weaker part of the citation, since Sr, Yb and Al+ groups all reach that range, and the durable claim is magic-wavelength trapping of many neutral atoms and its realisation as an accuracy-limited clock. That also answers the chair's question about why Katori and Ye and not the others: the concept is Katori's and the first full realisation at the limit is Ye's, whereas the other groups reproduced and extended it. I accept her point that the comb overlap is small, and that waiting for a metrological decision is not a scientific criterion.

responses.point: Danielsson holds that the experimental Higgs discovery is the most consequential result on the shortlist and that recognition is overdue, with Della Negra, Jenni and Virdee standing for ATLAS and CMS, while conceding that spokespersons and accelerator leaders have comparable claims.
responses.response: Nothing in the first round has changed my view that the discovery is the most consequential result on the list, and I do not dispute that it is overdue. His own concession, that spokespersons at the time of discovery, detector pioneers and accelerator leaders have comparable claims, is exactly why I cannot support the three names yet: no principle in the files separates these three from several others. I said I would reconsider if someone offered a defensible rationale. The chair asks for a decisive individual contribution, and I have not seen one, so I keep B012 outside my configuration. I would count it as a prize for a later year if the committee can settle the attribution rule.

responses.point: Eriksson now regards his rank of B029 as too low and would support it as a prize, but he still thinks DMFT is the more fundamental new idea and that part of the lattice clock's recognition follows from the 2005 and 2012 prizes.
responses.response: I value his willingness to say he would support B029, and I accept that DMFT is a deeper conceptual advance; I defer to him on the physics. But the question for this vote is whether the credited set is defensible, and he himself calls Metzner's omission a real gap in B035. A concept as fundamental as he describes is harder to prize fairly when the first step in the infinite-dimension limit is outside the three names. On his remaining point, I disagree that the clock simply follows from 2005 and 2012. The lattice scheme solves a separate problem, which is how to get large atom number without motional shifts, and that is what changed stability.

responses.point: Olsson places B018 as a candidate for a later year, because the 2012 prize is closer to it than any earlier prize is to the lattice clock and because Blatt alone cannot stand for the experimental gate demonstrations, and she records that I am a Chalmers colleague.
responses.response: I accept both objections to my own opening choice and they are the reasons I moved B018 behind the clocks. I would still keep B018 as my first fallback and not defer it entirely, because the Cirac-Zoller proposal is a distinct conceptual step that the 2012 citation did not cover, but only if the citation is written to say what is new beyond Wineland and Haroche and the NIST and Monroe credit is dealt with. I record her note about Chalmers and thank her for weighing my view on its merits; as I state in my conflict note, I have no link to the clock candidates.

uncertainties: Whether the committee judges the lattice clock sufficiently distinct from the comb and ion-control prizes; I judge that it is, but I accept that this is a judgement the citation has to carry.

Whether Katori and Ye can be defended, against Lemonde, Ludlow, Lisdat and the Yb and Al+ groups, as the originators and first realisers; I rely on the committee record rather than a private review of priority.
Whether to wait for the redefinition of the second; I do not think it is a scientific criterion, but others weigh it differently.

If B029 fails, whether B018 can be written to separate it from the 2012 prize and to handle NIST and Monroe credit, or whether B031 is mature enough given the open question of the correlated-state mechanism.
statement.conflict_note: I direct the Wallenberg Centre for Quantum Technology and work in superconducting circuits and waveguide QED, so I have professional proximity to B004 (circuit QED) and some to B018 (trapped-ion quantum computing) as neighbouring quantum-computing platforms. I would recuse myself from any deliberation that turns on B004. Chalmers colleagues and frequent co-authors named in my profile are not credited names for any shortlisted candidate. My profile records no connection to Katori, Ye or the optical clock community, so no specific conflict is apparent for B029. Olsson has noted that I am a Chalmers colleague, and I record that.
